LOCAL FISHER

TIME: May 12, 2025, 19:30. A volunteer receives a screenshot of a maritime notice concerning a berth project in Weitou Bay. It announces underwater blasting work for the following day.

The public notice can prove that relevant parties announced planned work. By itself, it cannot prove that the work later took place or that Chinese white dolphins were affected. Check the original webpage before deciding how to document the site.

TIME: May 13, 2025, 18:35. Construction vessels remain offshore, and engine noise and metal impacts can be heard from land. The player stops on the public shoreline and does not enter the project area.

A photograph can record the sea surface, construction vessels, and fixed landmarks. It cannot show underwater conditions, prove on its own that blasting is taking place, or prove that an animal was injured by that day's work.

PLAYER: Hello. I volunteer with a tidal observation station. Did you notice anything today—anything you saw, heard, or found different from usual?

FISHER: I heard two deep, muffled sounds in the afternoon. I was on shore and could not see below the surface, so I cannot say for certain what they were. Since last year, I have occasionally heard people mention sounds like that, but this was the first time I heard them myself. I did not dare stay to watch; I left quickly.

PLAYER: Did you see any white dolphins nearby?

FISHER: Yes, nearby. Not long after the sounds, several surfaced in the area. They were white with a fin on the back, so I recognized them. But I did not see clearly how many there were or whether any were injured.

This is an account from one witness. It can preserve an individual's experience, but it cannot independently confirm the source of the sounds, the number of blasts, the animal species, or causation. Keep the record anonymous and do not record the witness's face. Separate “heard directly,” “did not see blasting,” “previously saw suspected white dolphins,” and “date unknown” into distinct fields.

The player returns to the office. News reports, agency responses, public project documents, site photographs, and witness testimony appear together. Preserve E01 through E06 in their original timeline and label each as a direct record, witness account, media report, or pending professional review. The story must not imply that the player alone necessarily caused any suspension of work.

CLAIM 1: Public information indicates that the project conducted two reef-blasting operations on May 13.

Notice E01 proves the plan. Media report E05 supports the statement that two operations were conducted. The conclusion must retain source attribution; the construction-vessel photograph E02 cannot be treated as evidence of blasting.

CLAIM 2: Blasting that day injured or killed Chinese white dolphins.

E03 is witness testimony, E04 is distant footage, and E06 says only that no casualty reports had been received at the time. There are no casualty records, professional examinations, or materials that support a causal link.

CLAIM 3: Chinese white dolphins appeared in Weitou Bay, so all construction there must be illegal.

The first part requires reliable species and location data. The second is a legal conclusion that cannot be drawn from a single sighting. Revise it to: “Signs of white dolphin activity make the project's risks and protective measures worthy of professional assessment.”

Public project documents, Chinese white dolphin conservation materials, and a teaching map are open together. General knowledge of risk can explain why an investigation is worthwhile, but it cannot replace evidence of harm in this case.

At this stage, you may raise questions for review but may not declare the assessment invalid or the project illegal: What area did the documents actually investigate, and by what methods? Do the original records behind the simulation log exist? Is the available information sufficient to determine whether there is a material gap between survey coverage and white dolphin activity?

The next day, the player stands before the evidence wall. Claims are on the left and source cards on the right; every card shows acquisition time, source type, and limitations. Before submission, complete the source, time, original link, and limitations for every file, then confirm anonymity and access boundaries.

The internal report form does not generate an accusation automatically. Its four fixed sections are: VERIFIED, REPORTED BY SOURCES, RISK QUESTIONS, and STILL UNKNOWN.

VERIFIED: A notice announced underwater work for the next day; the player documented construction vessels from a public shoreline and preserved distant footage.
REPORTED BY SOURCES: An anonymous fisher said they heard two muffled sounds; media coverage relayed statements attributed to department staff.
RISK QUESTIONS: The Chinese white dolphin is a Class I nationally protected wild animal. Underwater blasting and habitat alteration are risks requiring professional assessment.
STILL UNKNOWN: The species in the footage, the animals' number and condition, the direct source of the sounds, whether assessment and protective measures were adequate, and the results of later independent monitoring.

On July 29, 2025, the player opens a case statement published by Friends of Nature. The organization says the project conducted another round of reef blasting in June and questions the environmental assessment and protective measures. These are an environmental organization's investigation and legal claims, not facts already confirmed by a court.

Later coverage reports that in August 2025 the court declined to docket the case on the ground that the social organization lacked standing. This is a procedural result, not a substantive ruling on whether the project was lawful, the assessment was adequate, or ecological harm occurred.

In September 2026, the player returns to the same public shoreline. Port facilities have taken shape, and a vessel passes in the distance. Public information relates to different dates and administrative matters; none of it establishes that the ecological dispute has received a substantive judicial ruling.

The player sets up a camera and records a new observation date, location, weather, and visibility. Clear echolocation clicks sound beneath the water as a pale silhouette passes far away.

Protecting marine animals means more than rescuing injured individuals. It also requires long-term understanding and protection of the habitats they depend on. One investigation cannot answer every question, but an accurate record is more useful than an exaggerated conclusion.
